thread.title: Alps Electric Looking To Recover After Swallowing A Sour Apple - Alps Electric Co. Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:APELY)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Alps Electric Looking To Recover After Swallowing A Sour Apple - Alps Electric Co. Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:APELY)
text:
As one of the companies that saw a significant hit to earnings and expectations from disappointing sales of Apple ’s ( AAPL ) iPhone X, Alps Electric ( OTCPK:APELY ) is in good company, but that’s hardly much comfort to investors. With weak camera actuators sales (tied to the X) leading to much lower guidance for the next fiscal year, Alps shares have lost about 10% of their value since my last update , though they are still up about 25% from my initial write-up and have done okay compared to a grab-bag of other Apple suppliers including Cirrus ( CRUS ), Dialog ( OTCPK:DLGNF ), and Skyworks ( SWKS ).
Alps needs a rebound in camera actuators to drive some near-term excitement, and recent reports have been somewhat encouraging. It also helps that Alps management took what I believe to be a big swing at its FY’19 guidance, leaving the door open for beat-and-raise quarters as the year moves on. What’s more, the long-term opportunity in auto components remains attractive. I’ve trimmed back my long-term revenue and FCF margins assumptions a bit, but the shares look interesting now for investors who can afford to wait for momentum to return to the financial results.
X Marks The Spot Like many companies supplying components for the iPhone X, the disappointing reception of this high-end phone has blown holes in the near-term model for Alps. Revenue from electrical components for the consumer business (which includes camera actuators for the iPhone X) was down 36% qoq in Alps’ fiscal fourth quarter, driving a sharp decline in margins.
With a couple of weaker than expected quarters in hand and revised expectations through the channel, Alps management seems to have decided to rip the band-aid off in one go. Management’s guidance for FY’19 calls for a 17% drop in operating income whereas the Street had been expecting a mid-single-digit increase. Weaker camera actuator sales expectations are driving this, and management has also elected to change how it depreciates its smartphone-related facilities and equipment in response – moving the depreciation period from five years to two years. That change alone accounts for a little more than half of the difference between management’s guidance and the prior average sell-side estimate, while revised forex expectations account for another 10%.
I’m not trying to sugar-coat the situation with camera actuators. This was supposed to be a significant near-term driver for Alps ahead of the multiyear opportunity in auto components (switches, encoders, sensors, connectivity, and so on). The adoption of OIS actuators is still a valid growth driver as more phone (and tablet) OEMs adopt the technology and move to dual OIS-actuated cameras, but it is going to take longer to develop due to the lower Apple-related sales. On the subject of Apple, though, March iPhone unit sales were stronger than generally expected and the June guide was also better than expected, so there could be some near-term upside relative to Alps management’s expectations (though likely more “less bad” than really good).
Auto Will Take Time To Scale Although consumer electronic component sales can be equal to or greater than auto electronic component sales in good quarters, I continue to believe Alps’ best long-term opportunities remain with the auto business.
Alps already generates close to a quarter of its revenue from switches, sensors, and modules for cars, as well as substantial percentages from door modules, instrument panels, and so on, in addition to in-car navigation and infotainment components. In the coming years, management expects to generate more than 70% of its revenue from the auto sector, with a greater mix of higher-value components for applications like powertrain (engine sensors and the like), ADAS, and communications, including millimeter-wave radar modules for advanced ADAS and V2X communications modules for vehicle communications.
Alps has also decided to change the structure of its pending deal for Alpine (a subsidiary focusing on car navigation systems). The two companies will be integrated as Alps Alpine under a single roof as opposed to a more separate arrangement. While it may seem like a largely cosmetic change, Japanese employment laws would have made it more difficult to quickly transfer personnel among the units under the prior structure. With a closer working relationship between these two units being one of the prime drivers of the deal (combining Alps’ expertise in component design and manufacturing and Alpine’s expertise in system integration), this seems like a strategically wise decision.
The Opportunity The sharp decline in camera actuators was arguably not a major surprise, though the subsequent slash-and-burn to FY’19 guidance was. Hopefully management’s guidance proves conservative, or at least reasonably accurate (meaning no significant downside from here), and actuator sales should start to recover from this lower base in the coming quarters. On the auto side, weaker build rates are a headwind at present and will delay some of the margin leverage investors have been looking for, but the auto opportunity at Alps is a multiyear opportunity.
Due in part to having somewhat low expectations to start with, my adjustments after Alps’ guidance aren’t so bad. My “same-store” revenue growth assumption from FY’18 onward is still around 3%, though I’ve chosen to take a more conservative view toward the margin leverage build. I still believe Alps will get its FCF margins into the mid-to-high single-digits, but the near-term outlook is weaker (FCF about 15% lower over the next three years than my prior expectations). Foreign exchange rates also make a difference, pushing my fair value for the ADR’s down into the mid-$60’s.
Investors should also note that the U.S. ADRs for Alps are illiquid; investors interested in the shares may want to consider owning the local shares or at least using limit orders for the ADRs.
The Bottom Line Alps is likely looking at least a couple of challenging quarters before actuator volumes recover and the overall financials start to look better. I do think expectations are now at a beatable level, but it’s going to take time for investors to trust this stock/company again. Still, for long-term investors who can afford to wait, the value here is interesting.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
